strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in language agent spatial reasoning: accumulating and propagating spatial inconsistencies across long horizons.
Well-motivated algorithmic framework that borrows sound principles from SLAM and database systems (reasoning history DAG, LCA-based error localization, and impact scoring).

Thorough evaluation spanning isolated algorithmic validation (without LLM confounds), synthetic random graphs, procedural text games (TextWorld), interactive fiction (cleaned MANGO), and literary text.

Commendable transparency regarding trade-offs, negative interactions (e.g., rollback thrashing under high error densities), and the over-generation of entities/edges in continuous literary descriptions.
weaknesses: The combined framework (VC+EI) does not consistently outperform Edge Impact (EI) ranking alone. In the ablation (Table 1) and MANGO experiments (Table 3), adding Version Control often degrades performance (e.g., CF rate drops from 95% to 50% on Topology 4, and 50% to 25% on Direction 8), indicating that LLM rollback/history integration can cause thrashing.

In the natural text evaluation (Dream of the Red Chamber), only recall is emphasized, while precision and F1 are omitted despite predicting ~4× the true number of nodes and edges (~24% precision), making the headline recall gains misleading.

The deterministic non-LLM reference (`heuristic_remove`) substantially outperforms all LLM repair variants in reducing residual conflicts (98 vs. 396 for the best LLM) while suffering comparable or fewer lost ground-truth edges (-56 vs. -86/-89 for GPT-5.5), raising questions about the practical necessity of LLM-based repair over symbolic graph algorithms.
The end-to-end natural text deployment is restricted to a very small sample (two chapters of a single novel) evaluated with a single LLM.

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing a key bottleneck in LLM-based navigation and spatial reasoning: detecting and resolving cascading spatial errors in long-horizon incremental mapping.

Principled algorithmic formulation combining temporal version control (Reasoning History DAG) with Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) candidate extraction and a PageRank-inspired Edge Impact Score for repair prioritization.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning synthetic controlled ablations, seven models from three major vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), procedurally generated TextWorld environments, interactive fiction walkthroughs (cleaned MANGO), and literary natural text.

Commendable transparency regarding trade-offs, negative results (e.g., performance degradation of VC+EI under high directional conflict density), and computational trade-offs between heuristic removal and LLM-driven preservation.
weaknesses: In the real-text deployment on Dream of the Red Chamber (Table 4), the large edge recall gain (+55.8 pp) comes at the expense of severe over-generation (~4x the ground-truth node and edge counts). Without reporting precision or F1 score, it is hard to assess whether the graph repair genuinely improves overall map quality or merely inflates recall via densification.

The full system (VC+EI) frequently underperforms Edge Impact ranking alone (EI) or even the unscaffolded baseline in several settings (e.g., Table 1 Topology 4: EI 95% vs. VC+EI 50%; Table 3 GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.5F), suggesting that the rollback/history mechanism can be unstable and prompt the LLM into destructive rewrite cycles.

The simple non-LLM baseline (heuristic_remove) resolves significantly more conflicts (98 residual conflicts) than any LLM-based repair method (best LLM is 396), highlighting that LLM repair agents frequently inject secondary conflicts during editing.

Real-world natural language evaluation is confined to a single two-chapter passage from one novel, making it difficult to assess generalizability across varied descriptive writing styles and spatial granularities.

strengths: Principled problem formulation: Tackling long-horizon consistency and spatial memory drift in LLM agents through structured graph representations and rectification is a relevant and important problem for spatial NLP and language-based agents.

Well-designed algorithmic components: Formulating error localization via Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) over the temporal Reasoning History DAG and prioritizing repairs using the PageRank-inspired Edge Impact Score are technically sound and intuitive ideas.

Extensive multi-environment and cross-vendor evaluation: The experiments cover synthetic graphs, procedurally generated TextWorld environments, interactive fiction from MANGO, and literary text, evaluating seven models across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

Transparency and self-critical analysis: The authors are candid about existing limitations, explicitly noting issues such as rollback thrashing in high-density error regimes and over-generation on natural language text.
weaknesses: Misleading evaluation metrics on natural text: In Table 4 (Dream of the Red Chamber), only recall is reported. LLM-MapRepair predicts 143 nodes and 144 edges against a 35-node, 34-relation ground truth (approx. 4x over-generation). Reporting high recall (+55.8 pp) without precision or F1 obscures the fact that precision is extremely low (~20-24%), making it questionable whether the resulting graph is practically useful.

Non-LLM heuristic baseline outperforms the proposed method: In Table 3 and Table A3, the simple non-LLM reference 'heuristic_remove' achieves significantly fewer residual conflicts (98 vs. 396 for best LLM mode) while actually preserving more ground-truth edges (-56 lost edges vs. -86 to -89 lost edges for GPT-5.5). This strongly weakens the empirical justification for the complex LLM-driven repair pipeline.

Mixed and negative contributions from the Version Control (VC) module: Across several benchmarks, adding Version Control (VC+EI) underperforms Edge Impact alone (EI) (e.g., Table 1 Topology 4 drops from 95% to 50%; Table 3 GPT-5.5 increases conflicts from 396 to 458). The authors note that the agent spends budget undoing partial rewrites, indicating that the integration of rollback mechanisms with LLM agent planning requires deeper architectural rethinking.

Narrow real-text evaluation and lack of downstream task validation: The real-text evaluation is limited to only two chapters of a single novel (Dream of the Red Chamber). Furthermore, the paper does not evaluate downstream task performance (e.g., path planning, QA, or navigation accuracy) to demonstrate that the repaired graphs actually improve agent reasoning.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in LLM-based spatial reasoning: long-horizon error accumulation and topological inconsistency during incremental map construction.

The proposed LLM-MapRepair framework is conceptually well-motivated, elegantly combining database/version control principles (commit history, rollbacks, causal tracing) with graph analysis (lowest common ancestor, reachability, conflict count, and usage scoring).

Presents a comprehensive ablation study comparing individual components (Edge-Impact Ranking vs. Version Control) across multiple LLMs, showing that the combination improves repair accuracy over ranking alone and significantly outperforms the unguided baseline.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream task evaluation: While the paper motivates incremental graph construction by citing limitations in answering navigation and shortest-path queries over long trajectories, the evaluation only measures intrinsic repair metrics (repair rate and edge accuracy) rather than downstream planning, localization, or navigation success on the constructed maps.

Discrepancies in data reporting: Figure A1 explicitly states in its caption that 'Naming conflicts are not observed', which directly contradicts Table A1 and Table A2 where numerous naming conflicts are documented (e.g., 72 in cutthroat, 24 in murdac, 8 in detective).

Missing operational and reproducibility details: The paper omits the exact LLM prompt designs, function-calling/tool-use specifications, and agent interaction protocols used to execute repair operations (`rollback_to`, `recall_step`, `diff`). Furthermore, the model designation 'GPT-4.1' in Table 2 and Table A4 is non-standard and unexplained.

Inefficient use of appendix space: Pages 22 to 32 consist almost entirely of an unannotated, raw text dump of the game walkthrough for 'Adventure' rather than providing deeper analysis, qualitative error breakdowns, or concrete execution traces of the repair mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in LLM-based spatial reasoning and interactive agents: the vulnerability of long-horizon incremental mapping to cascading structural and topological errors.

The proposed framework is conceptually well-motivated, bringing proven ideas from SLAM, transaction logging (WAL), and knowledge graph editing—such as versioning, LCA-based error localization, and edge impact scoring—into LLM agent memory management.

The ablation experiments (Table 1) provide clear evidence of the complementary nature of the components: Edge Impact Ranking substantially speeds up conflict resolution, whereas Version Control provides the necessary context to achieve significantly higher repair accuracy.
The evaluation covers multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-Haiku), demonstrating consistent improvements over the unassisted baseline.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies exclusively on intrinsic map repair metrics (repair rate, accuracy, loop count) and does not demonstrate whether the repaired graphs actually translate to improved downstream task performance (such as navigation success rate, goal-reaching efficiency, or path-planning query accuracy).

The PageRank connection in Section 2.3 is tenuous; while cited as theoretical motivation, the resulting score function (Equation 2/4) is simply an unweighted sum of three heuristic counters after min-max normalization.

The dataset refinement of MANGO involved heuristic filtering and manual/semi-automated removal of 160 edges. While removing non-topological actions (e.g., 'pray') is well-justified, altering ground-truth edges makes comparisons against prior published baselines difficult unless the dataset and evaluation code are rigorously standardized and released.

The framework assumes relatively rigid spatial semantics (such as deterministic bidirectional edges and strictly grid-like or tree-like constraints), which may limit applicability to non-Euclidean, dynamic, or non-deterministic environments.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely challenge in LLM-based spatial reasoning: the cascading accumulation of topological errors during long-horizon exploration and incremental mapping.
The proposed framework thoughtfully combines concepts from SLAM and knowledge graph management (version control, rollbacks, and lowest common ancestor tracing) to enable targeted graph rectification.
The systematic cleaning and refinement of the MANGO benchmark to eliminate non-topological actions and existing spatial contradictions is a valuable contribution for the community.
The ablation experiments (Table 1) clearly demonstrate the complementary benefits of historical version tracking and edge impact prioritization in resolving conflicts.
weaknesses: Lack of downstream task evaluation: While the paper motivates the framework through navigational query answering and shortest-path planning, the experimental evaluation is limited strictly to intrinsic graph repair statistics (repair rate, loops, accuracy). It remains unproven whether the repaired graphs actually improve agent navigation, localization, or downstream question answering.

Vague experimental and evaluation details: The manuscript does not formally define how 'Accuracy' is verified against ground truth (e.g., graph edit distance, isomorphism, or exact edge match). Furthermore, the exact prompt, action space, and decision loop used by the LLM during the 'Fix the error' step and baseline configurations are not provided.

Format and page limit violations: The main paper body extends to 16 pages before the references, drastically exceeding standard ACL/ARR page constraints (typically 8 pages for long papers). Moreover, Appendix 6.2 consists of 12 pages of uncurated raw text transcripts from an interactive fiction playthrough without meaningful synthesis.

Overstated theoretical claims: Section 2.3 frames the edge scoring heuristic as theoretically motivated by PageRank, yet the implementation is simply an unweighted linear sum of three normalized static structural counts (reachability, conflict count, usage). Additionally, referring to 'GPT-4.1' in Table 2 is ambiguous and non-standard without specific model version/API identifiers.
